_comment: The applications the demo site is built from, and what each one is
supposed to print. One entry here is the whole of adding a build: it
feeds scripts/stage_site.sh, the _site/manifest.json the page reads its
menu from, and scripts/check_site.mjs, which is what CI runs.
app: a path under the west workspace. {module} is this repository.
expect: substrings that must all appear in the output. This is the
acceptance criterion, so it should name what the application is for,
not merely that it started.
endless: the application never finishes, so the harness gives up at
max_time_ms and exits 2. Expected, not a failure.
title: a short name for the menu. hint: one sentence the page shows
while it runs, saying what it does or what to do. Both required.
uses: what of the board the page should show: leds, buttons, flash
(the Erase flash button), terminal (the output reads the keyboard: a
cursor, and keys go to the guest's UART), accel (the Tilt pad, which
sets what the emulated accelerometer reads). A display build is marked by
display instead. Checked against each build's .config.
interactive: the application waits for a person. The page forwards
keystrokes on the output to the guest's UART.
clock: virtual (default) or paced. Paced lets virtual time pass at the
rate it claims, so a sample that blinks once a second can be watched.
The page honours it; the checks do not, because the guest sees the
same clock either way and waiting would only make CI slower. Every
interactive build is paced, so a person sees real timestamps and the
guest does not race ahead while waiting for them.
max_time_ms is what the page gives a build; ci_max_time_ms overrides it
for the checks, which have no one watching.
ci_gpio: scripted input-pin events, so a sample that waits for a
button can be checked unattended and deterministically.
upstream: unmodified upstream Zephyr code. false for this port's own
tests, which prove the port rather than the samples.
kind: sample or test. The score in ROADMAP.md counts upstream samples,
because the samples are the teaching material. An upstream test suite
is evidence for the port and is not a sample.
persist_expect / persist_absent: for a build that keeps
simulated flash. The browser check runs it, reloads the page and runs
it again: the second run must print persist_expect and must not print
persist_absent, which is what it prints when the flash is empty.
display: the build draws on the board's display, so the page shows its
canvas and check_site.mjs screenshots the last frame, which must show
at least display.colors_at_least distinct colours.
ci_touch: scripted touches, <ms>:<x>,<y> in display pixels: run.mjs
--touch for the Node check, a real click on the canvas for the
browser check.
ci_accel: scripted accelerometer readings, <ms>:<x>,<y>,<z> in m/s^2:
run.mjs --accel for the Node check. The browser check drags the Tilt
pad instead, which cannot land on exact values, so what the script
should produce goes in ci_expect, which only the Node check reads.
A reading at 0 ms arrives before the guest has booted, as the page's
first one does, before the driver has enabled its interrupt.
args: build arguments, only ever the upstream entry's own extra_configs
(the LVGL demos app chooses its demo that way).
lesson: a guided lesson, as a list of steps the page shows one at a
time, each written like a hint. Nothing checks that a step was
followed; the browser check follows them to see that they still hold.
threads_expect: substrings the thread table must show at some point in
the Node check's run (run.mjs --threads), for a lesson that relies
on what the table says.
boards: two boards joined by an Ethernet link, or by a radio between
their Bluetooth controllers, in place of app. Each has an app, a
label, and what a build has: args (with -DSNIPPET=wasm-ethernet, which
gives it the link, or -DSNIPPET=wasm-bt, the radio), uses, ci_stdin and
expect, which is checked against that board's own output. ci_stdin is
typed into that board's own shell: stdin for the first, run.mjs
--peer-stdin for the second, and its own terminal on the page. They are
built as <name>-0 and <name>-1. The page runs them side by side; the
Node check runs them with run.mjs --peer. The two boards run on one
clock (host/pair.mjs), so a pair is as repeatable as one board: the
Node check runs each pair twice and requires the same output.
A board's args may only turn the link on and set addresses, ports and
IP versions (PAIR_ARG in apps.py); overrides says in words what was
set, and the page shows it. start_after_ms powers a board on after the
other, as a client is plugged in after its server; the first board is
the one that starts first. ci_link_frames_at_least is how many frames
(or radio packets) the browser check wants each way (default 100); 0
for a radio pair where one board only listens, whose expect shows
what it heard.
ci_stdin_at_ms holds
the first board's typing until that much guest time has passed
(run.mjs --type-at), for a command whose answer needs the board to
have finished setting up. Otherwise a line is typed as soon as the
shell's prompt shows, as twister's shell harness types.
uplink: one board on a real network, through a relay that speaks v86's
wsproxy protocol (host/uplink.mjs). Built with -DSNIPPET=wasm-ethernet
and nothing else; the relay's DHCP gives it an address. The page
offers an Uplink field for it, off until someone gives it a relay's
URL, and the checks run it only when given one with --uplink-relay.
Real peers follow the wall clock, so it is paced and not repeatable.
lan: one board on the host's own network (host/lan.mjs): lwIP at
192.0.2.2 answers ARP, ping, DHCP, DNS, SNTP, TFTP, HTTP, WebSocket,
CoAP over TCP, FTP, MQTT and MQTT-SN (host/lan_services.mjs), on the
board's clock, so the run is as repeatable as any other; check_site.mjs
runs it twice and requires the same output. true, or an object with
dial:
[{"at_ms", "port", "path"}] for a sample that is a server (the LAN
connects at that guest time and asks for the path, "/" unless given)
and ping: [ms], times at which the LAN pings the board. Built with
-DSNIPPET=wasm-ethernet and what PAIR_ARG allows, with overrides saying
so. An entry with lan and uplink runs on the LAN unless someone gives
the page a relay.
lan_expect: substrings the LAN's own log must show, for a sample whose
output cannot say what happened: a server does not print what it
served, nor a filter what it dropped. The log is the lines stamped
[lan 00:00:02.000,300] with the time on the board's clock, on stderr
under run.mjs and in the terminal on the page.

builds.name: hello
builds.title: Hello world
builds.hint: Prints a greeting and exits.

builds.name: sync
builds.title: Synchronization
builds.hint: Two threads take turns with a semaphore, forever; the speed control changes their pace.
expect: thread_a: Hello World from cpu 0 on wasm_node!
thread_b: Hello World from cpu 0 on wasm_node!

builds.name: sem
builds.title: Kernel semaphores (ztest)
builds.hint: Runs upstream's semaphore test suite.

builds.name: slice
builds.title: Time slicing
builds.hint: Two threads at the same priority share the CPU by time slice.
expect: PASS: both threads ran, so preemption works

builds.name: blinky
builds.title: Blinky
builds.hint: LED 0 toggles once a second; the speed control changes how fast a second is.

builds.name: button
builds.title: Button
builds.hint: Press Button 0: LED 0 is lit for as long as it is held. The sample prints each button's input key code (11 for Button 0, 2 for Button 1) and the time in cycles, a million a second.

builds.name: power
builds.title: Power states
builds.hint: Sleeps for 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 s, and the kernel picks a deeper power state for each longer sleep. Then latency constraints rule the deeper states out, one by one. The sample's own hooks print each state as it is entered.
expect: Finished, we should now enter STANDBY

builds.name: accel
builds.title: Accelerometer
builds.hint: Drag the dot in Tilt to tilt the board. The reading comes from the real bmi160 driver, reading an emulated chip over an emulated I2C bus.

builds.name: entropy
builds.title: Entropy API (ztest)
builds.hint: Runs upstream's entropy driver test suite.

builds.name: philo
builds.title: Dining philosophers
builds.hint: Six threads contend for forks, forever; the speed control changes their pace.
lesson: Press Run if it is not running yet. Six philosophers share six forks, and each philosopher is a thread. The table under the output is the kernel's own list of threads: watch each one think, wait for a fork, and eat.
Press Pause. Nothing runs now, and nothing is lost: every thread keeps its state and its stack. The table is the kernel's answer, asked of the guest between two context switches, not a guess.

Press Step. The kernel runs to its next stop: a context switch, or waking from idle. The arrow marks the thread that holds the CPU. Philosophers 0 to 5 start at priorities 3, 2, 1, 0, -1 and -2, which the output shows as `P:` for preemptible and `C:` for cooperative. The lower number runs first, and a cooperative thread, once running, keeps the CPU until it waits for something.

Find a philosopher whose state is `pending`. The waiting-for column says which fork, a mutex, it is waiting for, and which philosopher holds it. Compare the holder's priority with the one it started at. A mutex lends its owner the priority of the most urgent thread waiting for it, so that the owner finishes and lets go sooner. That is priority inheritance.

Why does this never deadlock? If each philosopher took the fork on one side and then waited for the other, all six could hold one fork each and wait forever. Here each takes the lower-numbered of their two forks first, so Philosopher 5 reaches for fork 0 before fork 5. A circle of waiting would need someone to hold a higher fork while waiting for a lower one, and no one ever does. See `philosopher()` in `samples/philosophers/src/main.c`.

Press Back to undo a step. The whole machine is one block of memory, so the page keeps a copy from before each step and puts it back. Step back to the moment a fork changed hands: the waiter leaves `pending`, and the holder's priority drops back to where it started.

builds.name: logger
builds.title: Logging
builds.hint: Exercises the logging subsystem and exits. Its speed estimate is meaningless here: logging takes no time on a virtual clock, and the sample's 32-bit arithmetic overflows.
expect: RUNNING LOGGER DEMO FROM KERNEL THREAD

builds.name: heap
builds.title: System heap
builds.hint: Allocates from a sys_heap and prints its statistics.
expect: allocated 156, free 36, max allocated 156, heap size 256

builds.name: dsp
builds.title: CMSIS-DSP moving average
builds.hint: Runs a ten-tap moving-average FIR filter from Arm's CMSIS-DSP library over a ramp, in plain C here rather than Arm's SIMD.

builds.name: nanopb
builds.title: Protocol buffers (nanopb)
builds.hint: Encodes a message with nanopb, decodes it again, and prints what came back. The C for the message was generated from a .proto file at build time.

builds.name: metairq
builds.title: Meta-IRQ dispatch
builds.hint: Measures how fast meta-IRQ threads preempt the rest.

builds.name: display
builds.title: Display
builds.hint: Draws upstream's display test pattern on the canvas.

builds.name: touch
builds.title: Touch events
builds.hint: Click or drag on the display to move the crosshair.

builds.name: lvgl
builds.title: LVGL widgets
builds.hint: Click and drag on the display; the output is a shell as well.

builds.name: lvgl-hello
builds.title: LVGL hello world
builds.hint: LVGL's hello world: a button, and a counter below it that counts seconds. Click the button to set the counter back to 0. The output is a shell as well: try `lvgl stats memory`.

builds.name: calculator
builds.title: SMF calculator
builds.hint: A desk calculator whose logic is a hierarchical state machine (the State Machine Framework), drawn with LVGL. Click its keys: each one is logged, with the state the machine is left in. It asks for CONFIG_DEBUG, so it is built for debugging, which on this board means more stack for every thread.

builds.name: nvs
builds.title: NVS in flash
builds.hint: Stores values in flash and reboots itself. Run it again — even after reloading the page — and the values are still there; Erase flash starts over.

builds.name: hsm
builds.title: Hierarchical state machine
builds.hint: Click the output, then type `hsm_psicc2 event A` (events A to I).

builds.name: shell
builds.title: Shell
builds.hint: Click the output, then type `help` and press Enter. This sample turns off the boot banner, so it starts at the prompt.

builds.name: echo-bot
builds.title: UART echo bot
builds.hint: Click the output, type a line and press Enter: the bot reads it a byte at a time in its UART interrupt and sends it back. The interrupt is real: the board raises it when your keys arrive.

builds.name: echo
builds.title: Echo over Ethernet (two boards)
builds.hint: Two boards on one link: the client echoes TCP and UDP off the server and counts what comes back. The server echoes quietly, so its terminal stays still; type `net iface` or `net ping 192.0.2.2` there to look at it.

builds.name: echo-async
builds.title: Echo, asynchronous server (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against echo_async, a single-threaded server that serves several clients with poll(). TCP only, so the client's UDP half reports that nothing came back.

builds.name: echo-select
builds.title: Echo, select() server (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against echo_async_select, the same server built on select(). TCP only, so the client's UDP half reports that nothing came back.

builds.name: echo-one
builds.title: Echo, one client at a time (two boards)
builds.hint: echo_client against the simplest echo server, which serves one TCP connection at a time. The client connects over IPv6 first, so its IPv4 connection waits in the backlog.

builds.name: coap
builds.title: CoAP client and server (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_client asks coap_server for resources over IPv6: GET, PUT, POST and DELETE, a 2 KB resource in 64-byte blocks, and an observed counter that the server pushes every 5 s.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and pointed at the server's CoAP port, [2001:db8::1]:5683; as shipped, both boards would be ::1 and the client would look for a server at ::2.

builds.name: coap-up
builds.title: CoAP upload (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_upload sends coap_server four PUTs over IPv6: two short, two in 128-byte blocks, which the server asks to have in 64s.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and the server's, 2001:db8::1, and its IPv4 is turned off: the server speaks only IPv6, and as shipped the client tries IPv4 first and waits minutes for each timeout.

boards.label: Client
expect: CoAP upload blockwise with callback done in

builds.name: coap-down
builds.title: CoAP download (two boards)
builds.hint: coap_download fetches a 2 KB resource from coap_server over IPv6, 64 bytes at a time.
builds.overrides: The client is given the address 2001:db8::2 and the server's, 2001:db8::1, and its IPv4 is turned off, as for the upload; and it asks for the server's large resource, since the file it names by default is not one coap_server has.

builds.name: http
builds.title: HTTP client and server (two boards)
builds.hint: http_client makes GET and POST requests of http_server over IPv4 and IPv6. The GETs succeed; the POSTs come back 404 or 405, because the client was written for a test server on a Linux host and its paths are fixed in its source. The server also has a shell: try `net iface` there.
builds.overrides: The server listens on port 8000, which the client has built in, rather than 80; and the client's addresses are swapped to 192.0.2.2 and 2001:db8::2, with the server as its peer.

builds.name: zperf
builds.title: zperf throughput (two boards)
builds.hint: Two copies of zperf, Zephyr's network throughput tool, one at each end of the link. Type `zperf udp download` on the server, then `zperf udp upload 192.0.2.1 5001 5 1K 100K` on the client; `zperf tcp download` and `zperf tcp upload 192.0.2.1 5001 5 1K` for TCP. The rates are those of two paced virtual boards in one browser tab, not of a real link.
builds.overrides: The client's addresses are swapped to 192.0.2.2 and 2001:db8::2, with the server as its peer.

boards.label: Server
boards.ci_stdin:
zperf udp download
zperf tcp download

boards.label: Client
boards.ci_stdin:
zperf udp upload 192.0.2.1 5001 2 256 50K
zperf tcp upload 192.0.2.1 5001 2 256

builds.name: mdns
builds.title: mDNS name lookup (two boards)
builds.hint: dns_resolve asks the local link who zephyr.local is, over IPv4 and IPv6 multicast, and mdns_responder answers with its addresses. Its plain DNS queries have no server to answer them and time out. Both boards have a shell: try `net dns zephyr.local` on the client.
builds.overrides: The client is given the addresses 192.0.2.2 and 2001:db8::2, and the responder's as its peer; as shipped, both boards would be 192.0.2.1 and 2001:db8::1.

builds.name: hr
builds.title: Bluetooth heart rate (two boards)
builds.hint: Zephyr's own Bluetooth host on both boards, over the H4 driver, to a controller the page emulates: the sensor advertises, the monitor scans, connects, finds the heart-rate service and subscribes, and a reading arrives every second.

builds.name: gatt-write
builds.title: Bluetooth GATT writes, encrypted (two boards)
builds.hint: The central connects to the first device it hears nearby, asks for security, and the two pair (Secure Connections, Just Works) and encrypt the link; then both write to each other as fast as the link allows and print the rate, while the peripheral asks for new connection parameters every few seconds.

builds.name: beacon
builds.title: Bluetooth beacon and observer (two boards)
builds.hint: A beacon advertises its name; an observer scans and reports what it hears, the advertisement and the scan response. Both run Zephyr's Bluetooth host over the H4 driver, to a controller the page emulates.

builds.name: http-get
builds.title: HTTP GET over the host's network
builds.hint: http_get looks up google.com and asks it for "/". Nothing leaves the page: the page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network, which answers the lookup with its own address and the request with a redirect, the answer upstream's own test expects, and says it was the one answering.

builds.name: http-srv
builds.title: A web server, asked by the host
builds.hint: dumb_http_server waits for a connection on port 8080. The page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network: a second into the run it connects and asks for "/", and the board sends its page back.

builds.name: tftp
builds.title: TFTP client
builds.hint: tftp_client reads file1.bin from a TFTP server at 192.0.2.2, prints it and writes a file back. The server is the page itself, playing a Linux host on a simulated network; nothing leaves the page.

builds.name: sntp
builds.title: SNTP client
builds.hint: sntp_client asks an SNTP server at 192.0.2.2 for the time, twice. The server is the page itself, playing a Linux host on a simulated network; its clock starts at 2026-01-01 00:00 UTC when the board's does. The simulated network speaks only IPv4, so the sample's IPv6 request fails.
builds.overrides: The client is pointed at the SNTP server 192.0.2.2; as shipped it asks pool.ntp.org, and has no DNS resolver to find it with.

builds.name: net-mgmt
builds.title: Network management events
builds.hint: net_mgmt listens on a network management socket while it adds an IPv6 address to its interface, waits for duplicate address detection, and removes it again, round and round, printing each event. The interface is plugged into the simulated network the page plays, a Linux host at 192.0.2.2, which answers nothing here: nobody else claims the address, so every check succeeds.

builds.name: stats
builds.title: Network statistics
builds.hint: The stats sample prints the network stack's counters every 30 s of guest time: packets sent and received per protocol, globally and for the interface. Its interface is plugged into the simulated network the page plays, a Linux host at 192.0.2.2, and the 42 bytes received are that host announcing itself.

builds.name: virtual
builds.title: Virtual network interfaces
builds.hint: The virtual sample stacks tunnel interfaces on its Ethernet interface, which is plugged into the simulated network the page plays, and prints what it attached to what. It reports its IPIP interface as -1 on every board: it looks for a device called "IP_tunnel", which Zephyr now names "IP_TUNNEL0".

builds.name: mqtt-pub
builds.title: MQTT publisher
builds.hint: mqtt_publisher connects to an MQTT broker at 192.0.2.2 and, over and over, pings it and publishes a message at each quality of service: at most once, at least once (acknowledged with PUBACK) and exactly once (PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP). The broker is the page, playing a Linux host on a simulated network; its lines show what it received.
lan_expect: MQTT zephyr_publisher published 15 bytes to sensors at QoS 2

builds.name: promisc
builds.title: Promiscuous mode
builds.hint: promiscuous_mode turns on promiscuous mode and logs every frame that arrives. The page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network, and pings the board at 1, 2 and 3 s: an ARP request (42 bytes), then three echo requests (98 bytes). The sample reads the IP header where the Ethernet header is, so it calls every frame "unknown address family", as it does on any Ethernet board. The page's own lines start `[lan` and the time on the board's clock, and appear as soon as they happen. The board's log lines appear a little after the time they carry, so a `[lan …]` line can come before a board line with an earlier time.

builds.name: pkt-filter
builds.title: Packet filter
builds.hint: pkt_filter installs packet filter rules. Its IPv4 rule lets a packet in only if the sender is not on its blocklist, which `net filter` shows as `ip src block[192.0.2.2,…]`, so IPv4 from 192.0.2.2 is dropped. That is the page, playing a Linux host on a simulated network, and it pings the board at 1 and 2 s: the board answers the ARP request but not the pings. Type `net filter` to see the rules.

builds.name: vlan
builds.title: VLANs
builds.hint: The vlan sample adds two VLAN interfaces, tags 100 and 200, on its Ethernet interface, each with its own IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The Ethernet interface is plugged into the simulated network the page plays, which has no VLANs of its own. Type `net vlan` or `net iface` to see them.

builds.name: prometheus
builds.title: Prometheus metrics
builds.hint: The prometheus sample serves a request counter at /metrics on port 80. The page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network, which leases the board its address by DHCP and, 2 s in, asks for /metrics as a Prometheus server would. Its log line shows the answer's status and size, not the metrics themselves.

builds.name: ftp
builds.title: FTP client
builds.hint: ftp_client adds FTP commands to the shell. The page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network, with an FTP server that takes any user and password. Click the output and try `net ftp connect anonymous guest 192.0.2.2`, then `net ftp ls`, `net ftp get readme.txt`, `net ftp cd pub` and `net ftp get hello.txt`. What you put there lasts for the rest of the run.
builds.ci_stdin:
net ftp connect anonymous guest 192.0.2.2
net ftp ls
net ftp get readme.txt
net ftp cd pub
net ftp get hello.txt
net ftp disconnect
expect: You can interact with FTP server via shell.
This is the FTP server of the page's simulated network
Hello from FTP on the page.

builds.name: dhcp
builds.title: DHCP client
builds.hint: dhcpv4_client asks for an address and prints its lease. The page plays a Linux host at 192.0.2.2 on a simulated network and hands it 192.0.2.1; nothing leaves the page. In its shell, try `net iface`, `net ping 192.0.2.2` or `net dns zephyrproject.org`. Uplink is optional and can stay empty. To put the board on a real network instead, start a relay on your machine with `ENABLE_WSS=false npx rootlessrelay` and set Uplink to ws://127.0.0.1:8086/: the relay's own network gives it 10.0.2.15, with 10.0.2.2 as its gateway.
